title: Japanese punctuation
summary: Most Japanese punctuation is a modern import with loose rules; only the full stop is structural.

blocks.text: Japanese marks like 、 and ？ mostly arrived about 150 years ago, partly to translate Western books. So, unlike in English, they have few firm rules. The exception is the full stop.

rows: a pause, wherever you like; no rules

blocks.text: The full stop tells you where a sentence ends

Japanese uses long modifiers: whole clauses that describe a noun. A clause that ends in a noun is a **modifier**, not a sentence. A real logical clause ends in one of two ways: with 。, or with a connector like て, から or けど.
First, a noun with a long modifier. It ends in a noun, so it says nothing yet.

blocks.en: the umbrella I picked up at the station yesterday (not a sentence)

blocks.text: Now add a topic and an engine, and it becomes a sentence.

blocks.jp: 昨日駅で拾って交番に届けた財布は、まだ見つかっていない。
blocks.en: The wallet that I picked up at the station yesterday and took to the police box has not been claimed yet.

cars.text: 昨日駅で拾って交番に届けた
cars.label: describer

blocks.text: Only 見つかっていない is the engine; 拾って and 届けた just describe 財布.
Here 拾って and 届けた do not make statements: they just describe 財布. Only the final 見つかっていない (before 。) is the sentence's engine.

The comma has no grammar: schools even discourage too many, because commas should not carry your meaning. Questions and statements have the same structure, so か, an ending の or a rising voice marks a question; ？ just shows that rising tone in text. Here the same words become a question by the mark alone.

blocks.en: Is the coffee hot? (the ？ shows the rising voice)

blocks.text: 「 」 mark speech (not thoughts). Dots beside a word in vertical text mean emphasis, like italics.

blocks.jp: 「早く行こう」と友達が言った。

items: **。** is the only structural mark: a logical clause ends before it or before a clause connector.
**？** marks a rising tone; **か** is not required to use it.

questions.note: The full stop ends a sentence.

options: No: a noun with a modifier
questions.note: Even with 。 it ends in a noun, so it says nothing yet.
questions.en: the movie I saw at the station

questions.note: ？ shows the rising tone of a question without か.

questions.prompt: 母は「行ってきます」と言った。
questions.note: 「 」 mark what someone says.

questions.instruction: What are 『 』 used for inside a 「 」 quote?
questions.note: Double quotes.

questions.prompt: Japanese commas follow strict rules for subordinate clauses.
questions.note: There are no comma rules; use them for pauses.

questions.instruction: Which word closes the first logical clause?
questions.prompt: 雨が降っているけど、出かける。
questions.note: けど is a clause connector.
questions.en: It's raining, but I'll go out.

questions.instruction: Which sentence ends in a noun and is still complete?
questions.note: Noun + だ is an engine, so the sentence is complete.
Only the last one ends with an engine; the others end in a noun even with 。.

questions.instruction: What does 読んだ do in this sentence?
questions.prompt: 昨日読んだ本は、とても面白かった。
questions.note: A clause ending in a noun's modifier form describes the noun.
questions.en: The book I read yesterday was very interesting.

questions.instruction: Which word is a clause connector (the clause can end there without 。)?
questions.note: から, て, けど and similar words connect two clauses.

questions.instruction: Tap the connector that ends the first clause
questions.note: から ends the first clause and joins it to the next.
questions.en: Since it rained, I stayed home.

questions.instruction: Tap the noun that 作った modifies
questions.note: 作った describes 料理.
questions.en: The food my friend made is delicious.

questions.instruction: Tap the engine of the whole sentence
questions.note: 買った only modifies 本; 読んだ is the real engine.
questions.en: I read the book I bought yesterday.

questions.prompt: The shop where I met my friend is old.
questions.note: 友達に会った modifies 店; 古い is the engine.
questions.en: The shop where I met my friend is old.

questions.prompt: The movie I saw yesterday was fun.
questions.note: 昨日見た modifies 映画; 楽しかった ends the sentence.
questions.en: The movie I saw yesterday was fun.

questions.prompt: I wrote a letter and sent it.
questions.note: 書いて is a clause connector; 送った ends the sentence.
questions.en: I wrote a letter and sent it.

questions.prompt: You must write ？ to ask a question in Japanese.
questions.note: か, an ending の or a rising voice also make a question; ？ is optional.

options: The word is in the past
questions.note: Questions and statements have the same structure; the tone shows a question.

questions.prompt: 妹が「ありがとう」と言った。
questions.note: 「 」 mark speech.

questions.prompt: A comma 、 can change the grammar of a Japanese sentence.
questions.note: Commas are only pauses.

questions.instruction: Which one ends with an engine before 。?
questions.note: Only 飲んだ is an engine; the others end in a noun.

questions.instruction: Tap the connector that ends the first clause
questions.note: けど ends the first clause and joins it to the next.
questions.en: The rain stopped, but the wind is strong.
